extracted.intended_audience: creative writers and literary readers interested in fairy-tale aesthetics and the philosophy of wonder
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and aesthetic principles for composing or evaluating fairy-tale–style literature and prose that evokes wonder, limits, moral shape, and a personal sense of meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairy-tale language to register distinctness and wonder
rubrics_metrics.description: Use fairy-tale phrasing (e.g., 'the sun shines because it is bewitched') not as mysticism but as a rational, agnostic way to express that one thing is quite distinct from another and to record astonishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton argues this language is not irrational: it expresses the clear perception that there is no necessary logical connection between paired phenomena (e.g., flying and laying eggs). Antipattern: confusing sentimental associative thinking (assuming a dreamy connection because two things are often seen together) with genuine imaginative distinctness. Scoring note: prose that shows a fresh sense of separateness and surprise scores highly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke the instinct of astonishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Good tales touch the ancient instinct of astonishment; stories should provoke the reader's wonder rather than merely explain it away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: children of different ages respond differently (a three-year-old is excited when told Tommy opened a door). Practical advice: favor incidents that restore the reader's astonishment about ordinary facts (making apples seem golden to refresh that they were green). Antipattern: over-explanation or demystification that kills astonishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform the ordinary by recollection or contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Make ordinary objects/events feel miraculous by casting them as refreshed memories or contrasts (e.g., apples golden to recall they were green; rivers run with wine to recall they run with water).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: use analogical or symbolic reversal to make common things appear newly marvelous. Scoring: imagery that causes readers briefly to 'remember' a prior astonished perception is effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Conditional Joy (virtue in an 'if')
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct visions of happiness that depend on a small withheld action or prohibition; wonder in the tale often hinges on a veto or condition ('You may live in a palace of gold... if you do not say the word "cow"').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a central fairy-tale device: great concessions are balanced by one forbidding condition. Use the conditional to create moral tension and narrative stakes. Examples from text: boxed gifts that, if tampered with, release evil; prohibitions whose breach causes disaster. Antipattern: presenting limitless joy without any binding condition or cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present law/obedience as mysterious duty rather than mere lawlessness
rubrics_metrics.description: Fairyland's apparent lawlessness is in fact strict obedience to an incomprehensible duty; stories should feature rules whose authority is mysterious yet binding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with political or intellectual revolts: fairyland's obedience is not rebellion founded on reason but submission to unknown commands (e.g., Cinderella's command to return by midnight). Use mystery of rule as moral texture; scoring favors believable mysterious obligations that generate consequences when broken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict joy as bright but brittle (fragility of happiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Portray happiness as dazzling yet fragile—like glass: brilliant, easily shattered by a careless act (glass slippers, glass castles, the image of heaven as terrible crystal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narratively foreground limits and the possibility of loss to make joy precious. Antipattern: treating happiness as indestructible or inexhaustible reduces poignancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require symbolic sacrifice or restraint as price for extraordinary joy
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptional pleasures ought to be paid for by ordinary moral restraint (e.g., paying for sunsets by not being Oscar Wilde—in Chesterton's phrase), or by ritual/sacrifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Story-builders should show characters observing restrictions or rituals that justify/earn their privileges. Antipattern: lovers of beauty who will not submit to any symbolic cost (they cheapen the wonder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat repetition/monotony as possible expression of phenomenal will, not mere mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Recurrent patterns in nature (e.g., daisies all alike, the sun rising every day) can be framed as deliberate 'encores' of a will or delight, not proof of lifeless determinism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting repeated actions, consider interpreting them as joyful choice rather than mechanical necessity—this preserves agency and wonder. Use imagery of 'God saying "Do it again"' as a model. Antipattern: reading repetition only as evidence of dead clockwork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey an implied storyteller/person behind the world
rubrics_metrics.description: If the world has meaning, it suggests a meaning-giver; stories should carry an inward sense of a personal authorial will or storyteller who 'meant' the events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic consequence: narratives that gesture toward a mind behind the scene (a storyteller, a maker) increase the sense of purpose. Scoring: works that make meaning feel personal and violent (intense) are preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor particularity and limits over cosmic gigantism
rubrics_metrics.description: Celebrate the smallness and particularity of things (cosmic cosiness, 'the poetry of limits' in Robinson Crusoe) rather than appealing to mere vastness as a spiritual argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: focus on intimate details, inventories, and the sense that the universe is a single jewel to be hoarded. Antipattern: using sheer magnitude (infinity, huge cosmos) to elide moral or poetic interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use inventories and salvaged lists to create emotional value
rubrics_metrics.description: A catalogue of salvaged objects (à la Robinson Crusoe) can make ordinary items heroic and emotionally charged, foregrounding how close they were to loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical device: include lists of small possessions or reminiscences of near-loss to heighten pathos and gratitude. Scoring: evocative inventories that imply wreck-and-salvage increase reader attachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embed morality in sacred/traditional forms rather than instrumental contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral behavior in strong tales arises from rituals, sacred customs, and loyalties (fighting for a shrine produces courage) rather than from conscious bargaining or utilitarian contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray moral codes as originating in devotion or holy duty (the Ten Commandments as regimental orders protecting an ark), so that virtues feel rooted and formative. Antipattern: depicting morality merely as a negotiated exchange ('I will not hit you if you do not hit me').

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain an authorial emotion of primary loyalty (patriotism) rather than cynical candidness
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper stance toward the world in story is a primary, pre-critical loyalty—loving the world before criticizing it; authors who use truth to undermine love (the 'uncandid candid friend') are morally suspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative voice should show that critique comes from love (wanting to improve), not from a secret pleasure in destruction. Antipattern: the pessimist who states facts to discourage or demoralize rather than to help.
